Title: Why do headlights look like starbursts at night? 3 everyday habits hurting your eyes

Description:
If headlights are turning into starbursts on your drive home and your eyes feel dry and gritty by the end of the day, it's not just "getting older" - a few everyday habits could be part of the problem.

Soda, fried and processed food, and late-night phone scrolling all quietly add oxidative stress and dryness to your eyes over time. Watch to find out why, and what to swap in instead.

platforms.title: Blurry Vision at Night? The Diet and Screen Habits Behind It
platforms.meta_description: Halos around lights and worse night vision aren't always just aging. Sugar, fried food, and dark-room scrolling all stress your eyes over time.
platforms.body_html:
Hazy vision, halos around headlights and streetlights, or a blurry, wavy patch in the center of your sight aren't automatically signs of aging catching up with you. Halos are one of the earliest signs of cataracts, while distorted central vision often points to macular degeneration — and if your eyes also feel gritty and your night vision has gotten noticeably worse, it's worth looking at diet and screen habits before assuming it's just age.

Sugary Drinks and Desserts: How AGEs Build Up in the Eye

Frequent sugary drinks and desserts cause repeated blood sugar spikes, and that steady stream of glucose drives the formation of advanced glycation end products, or AGEs — compounds formed when sugar molecules bind to proteins. Research on human lenses has found AGE levels several times higher in cataract-affected lenses than in clear ones, and AGEs have also been linked to progression of age-related macular degeneration. When AGEs accumulate in the lens, the normally transparent proteins stiffen and lose clarity, scattering incoming light — which is part of why halos and glare become more noticeable at night. This isn't limited to people with diabetes; a diet consistently high in added sugar can push this process along even in otherwise healthy eyes.

Fried and Ultra-Processed Food's Link to Late Macular Degeneration

A University at Buffalo analysis of nearly two decades of dietary data from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study found that people who ate a diet heavy in red and processed meat, fried food, refined grains, and high-fat dairy — a so-called "Western" pattern — were about three times more likely to develop late-stage age-related macular degeneration than those who didn't, though the link to early AMD was weaker. A more recent UK Biobank study of over 150,000 adults reached a similar conclusion from a different angle: a higher share of ultra-processed foods in the diet was significantly associated with greater risk of both AMD and cataract. Repeatedly heated cooking oil produces oxidized fats that promote oxidative stress, which can damage the tiny blood vessels feeding the retina over time.

Scrolling in the Dark and Why Your Eyes Feel Gritty

Scrolling on your phone in a dark room, especially right before bed, takes a toll too. According to the American Academy of Ophthalmology, people normally blink around 15 times a minute, but that rate can drop to as low as 5 to 7 times a minute while focused on a screen. Blinking less often means the tear film covering the eye doesn't get refreshed as frequently, which leaves eyes dry, gritty, and irritated — the hallmark of digital eye strain. Doing this in a dark room adds a second problem: the contrast between a bright screen and a dark room forces the pupils to work harder, and the resulting eye fatigue can compound next-day symptoms like blurred or strained vision.

What Actually Helps

  • Add dark leafy greens — Kale and spinach are rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, the two carotenoids that make up the eye's macular pigment. In the NIH-funded AREDS2 trial, a daily combination of 10 mg lutein and 2 mg zeaxanthin was linked to roughly a 26% lower risk of AMD progressing to a more advanced stage.
  • Swap fried food for oily fish — Salmon, mackerel, and other oily fish are rich in omega-3 fatty acids, which several studies, including analyses published in JAMA Ophthalmology, have linked to a reduced risk of AMD progression when paired with a diet rich in lutein and zeaxanthin.
  • Follow the 20-20-20 rule — The American Optometric Association recommends looking at something roughly 20 feet (6 meters) away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes. This gives the eye's focusing muscles a break and tends to reset your blink rate, helping restore the tear film.

The Bottom Line

None of this means you need to cut out sugar, fried food, or your phone entirely. What matters more is the pattern: frequent sugary drinks, a diet heavy in fried and ultra-processed food, and long stretches of screen time in the dark all add up to more oxidative stress and less tear film stability for your eyes. Swapping in dark leafy greens, choosing oily fish over fried food more often, and practicing the 20-20-20 rule are small, well-supported changes. This article is for general information only and isn't a substitute for professional care — if symptoms like halos, night vision loss, or persistent dryness continue, see an ophthalmologist.
